issues.issue: The purpose clause defines "the Business" only as "Spanish language and bilingual print and media business," a phrase with no product, geographic or market boundary. Because that defined term drives the exclusivity in the LSB non-compete (c017) and the joint-pursuit promise (c011), its outer limit is left to argument.

Giving DMSA two of three board seats vests it with complete control of management, which sits uneasily with c004's allocation to LSB of day-to-day operations, hiring and joint development of long-term strategy. A court would have to decide which management power controls when the board and the Publisher disagree.

"Publisher" is a bare title: the provision fixes no term, no authority and no employment relationship, and the word is not defined anywhere in the agreement. Whether it creates a protected position (or any position at all) that DMSA could not remove is left open.

The grant to LSB of authority to manage day-to-day operations and to recruit and hire employees and contractors cannot be squared with c006, which subjects all expenditures to DMSA's concurrence, or with c020's budget restriction. A court would have to decide whether LSB could hire anyone at all without DMSA's assent.

"Will not contribute any cash to initiate the LLC" is limited by the word "initiate" and says nothing about later cash calls or about what LSB does give for her 49%. The temporal boundary of the acknowledgment, and whether services are her consideration, are both left unstated.

Requiring DMSA's concurrence for "all expenditures" cannot be squared with c020, which permits members to incur costs so long as they accord with the approved budget, nor with c004's grant of day-to-day management to LSB. Whether budgeted spending still needs item-by-item DMSA assent is unresolved.

DMSA's funding obligation is measured only by "an amount that DMSA deems appropriate," setting no floor and arguably making the promise illusory, while the parenthetical lets internal labor and overhead of DMSA staff count as contributed capital. Both the amount owed and what qualifies as "initial capital" are left to DMSA's say-so.

The clause is grammatically broken — "requiring approval by the Board of Directors issuing any additional membership interests" omits the connective, so it is unclear whether the Board must approve issuances or is itself the issuer. It also only promises a future agreement, leaving the right of first refusal's terms unspecified.

Pro rata distribution of all profits the board decides to distribute cannot be squared with c019, which routes amounts paid by clients first to out-of-pocket costs and then entirely to DMSA to repay its initial capital before anything is shared by interest. Which of the two governs a given dollar of profit is left unresolved.

The mandatory annual tax distribution conflicts with c019, which places the same tax payment third in a waterfall behind full repayment of DMSA's initial capital, and with c009's board discretion over distributions. A court would have to decide whether the tax distribution is owed even when the waterfall never reaches step three.

The promise that the parties "shall through the LLC jointly pursue the Business" cannot be squared with c013 and c014, which free DMSA and its principals of any duty to bring business to the LLC and let them keep and originate competing media and advertising clients for themselves. Whether c011 imposes any enforceable duty on DMSA at all is the question.

The acknowledgment that DMSA's principals may hold interests "whether similar to the LLC's Business or not" contradicts the joint-pursuit obligation in c011 and the exclusivity imposed on LSB in c017. The instrument does not say how far this carve-out cuts into the venture's own field.

The disclaimer of any obligation to originate or assign business for the LLC cannot be squared with c015, in which DMSA agrees to use diligent efforts to direct appropriate business to the Company. A court would have to decide whether c015 adds a duty or is wholly negated by this sentence.
